content:
A European team of physicists has calculated that, under certain conditions, a rapidly spinning black hole could split into two separate black holes

A team of scientists in Europe has calculated that, under certain conditions, a black hole could split in two, Universe Today reports. Given the extremely strong gravity of black holes, the idea that any force could tear one apart seems almost impossible. Nevertheless, a team led by Francesco Sannino of the University of Naples Federico II and the Centre for Quantum Field Theory at the University of Southern Denmark, together with Giacomo Cacciapaglia of the Laboratory of Theoretical and High Energy Physics, Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, has carried out a series of calculations demonstrating how such a process might occur.

According to the study, the two resulting black holes must be able to move apart rather than immediately merge back together. “When we impose this requirement, the window largely closes again, except perhaps for black holes spinning close to the maximum possible rate,” Sannino explained. If such a separation were to occur, the black hole’s event horizon would take on a shape resembling a pair of trousers, with two separate ‘legs’. This is why the team has called the phenomenon ‘pants topology’.

One of the main obstacles to such a process is entropy, a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements of a system that appear identical from the outside. In an ordinary, non-rotating black hole, splitting would reduce its entropy, making the process thermodynamically improbable. However, a rapidly spinning black hole changes the relationship between mass, angular momentum and entropy, potentially making fragmentation theoretically possible. The two ‘twin’ black holes would need to move apart rapidly while preserving the momentum and velocity of the original.

No such event has ever been observed, and the idea remains largely theoretical. “We still cannot give a single probability for a black hole splitting. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein’s theory, and we are working to quantify this,” Sannino explained.

“We expect small primordial black holes to be more likely to split than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may be able to detect such a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT could search for signals from small black hole fragments that might form during mergers.” | BGNES
